title: What models can and can't do
objectives: say what a hallucination is and why it happens
say why counting and arithmetic are weak
say that nothing is remembered between calls
check an answer instead of trusting it

steps.instruction: Ask it something it has no idea about. It will still answer.
body: Last lesson: it picks the next likely token, every time, no exceptions.
There is no token that means "I have no idea". Nothing in the loop can stop and refuse.
So when it has nothing to draw on, it produces the next likely token anyway.
steps.keypoint: It never runs out of answer. That is the whole problem.

steps.instruction: One of these is real. The other is invented. Can you tell from the answer?

sides.label: Learned it
sides.code: console.log("The capital of Canada is Ottawa.");
sides.output: The capital of Canada is Ottawa.

sides.label: Made it up
sides.code: console.log("The capital of Canada is Kingsport.");
sides.output: The capital of Canada is Kingsport.

body: Same confidence. Same grammar. Same tone.
Nothing in the wording tells you which one to trust.
steps.keypoint: A wrong answer is built exactly like a right one, so it sounds exactly like one.

steps.instruction: That is called a hallucination. It is not lying.
body: Lying needs knowing the truth and choosing otherwise. Nothing here knows anything.
Where the training text was thick, the likely next tokens are the true ones.
Where it was thin, the likely next tokens are just plausible. The machinery does not change.
steps.keypoint: A hallucination is the same process running where the training data was thin.

steps.instruction: Here is a question it fails that a six-year-old does not.
body: How many r's are in strawberry? Models get this wrong all the time.
Remember A1.1: it never saw the letters. It saw the tokens str, aw, berry.
Asking it to count letters is asking it to count something it cannot see.
steps.keypoint: It cannot count letters because letters are not what it reads.

steps.instruction: The model gets this wrong. Code does not. What does this print?
steps.after: Three. Two lines, right every single time, and it costs nothing.
steps.why: Three r's. Code counts letters exactly, every time, because it can actually see letters.

body: A model produces the digits that usually follow that sum. It is not calculating.
Small sums it has seen a million times, it gets right. Unusual ones it does not.
Your computer already multiplies perfectly. Use the model for language, use code for numbers.
steps.keypoint: Language to the model. Numbers to the code.

steps.instruction: Deal each job to whichever one is actually good at it.

items.text: rewrite this paragraph to be friendlier
suggest three names for a project
explain this error message in plain words
check whether an email address contains an @

steps.after: The pattern: fuzzy and about meaning goes left, exact and countable goes right.
steps.keypoint: If code can do it exactly, code should do it.

steps.instruction: Now the one that surprises people building their first app.
body: Two separate calls. The second one contains one message, and it does not mention a name.
Nothing carries over. No session, no history, no memory of you at all.
Whatever it answers to the second call, it is not remembering.
steps.keypoint: Nothing is remembered between calls. Each one starts from nothing.

steps.instruction: So what comes back from that second call?
steps.code:
const call1 = { messages: [{ role: "user", content: "My name is Ada." }] };
const call2 = { messages: [{ role: "user", content: "What is my name?" }] };
opts: Ada, because it remembers a moment ago
An error, because there is no name in the call
A guess, worded as confidently as a real answer
steps.why: It cannot error, because nothing is malformed. It cannot know, because the name is not in the call. So it does the only thing it does: produces a likely answer. That is a hallucination arriving in a completely ordinary way.
steps.after: Two failure modes, one cause. No memory plus never says no equals confident nonsense.
steps.keypoint: Missing context does not produce an error. It produces a made-up answer.

steps.instruction: So the rule for building with this: verify anything you can verify.
body: If the answer must be one of a known set, check it is in the set.
If it names a user or a lesson, look the id up before you use it.
If it writes code, run it.
The check is usually two lines, and it is the difference between a demo and a feature.
steps.keypoint: Anything checkable, check. Never let the model be the only thing standing between wrong and shown.

steps.instruction: Fernland does not exist. What comes back?
steps.after: Fernland does not exist. It answered anyway, in one word, exactly as asked.
steps.why: It cannot refuse and it cannot error, so it produces a plausible name. In one word, exactly as instructed. That is a hallucination.

steps.instruction: So you check it against a list you control.
steps.after: The model was confident. Your two lines were right.
body: The model was confident and wrong. Two lines caught it.
unavailable is a real answer your app can show. A made-up city is not.
